verses.text: When Jeremiah had finished speaking to all the people all the words of Yahweh their God, with which Yahweh their God had sent him to them, even all these words,

then Azariah the son of Hoshaiah, and Johanan the son of Kareah, and all the proud men spoke, saying to Jeremiah, “You speak falsely. Yahweh our God has not sent you to say, ‘You shall not go into Egypt to live there;’
but Baruch the son of Neriah has turned you against us, to deliver us into the hand of the Chaldeans, that they may put us to death, and carry us away captive to Babylon.”
So Johanan the son of Kareah, and all the captains of the forces, and all the people, didn’t obey Yahweh’s voice, to dwell in the land of Judah.
But Johanan the son of Kareah, and all the captains of the forces, took all the remnant of Judah, who had returned from all the nations where they had been driven, to live in the land of Judah;

the men, and the women, and the children, and the king’s daughters, and every person who Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard had left with Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan; and Jeremiah the prophet, and Baruch the son of Neriah;
and they came into the land of Egypt; for they didn’t obey Yahweh’s voice: and they came to Tahpanhes.
Then Yahweh’s word came to Jeremiah in Tahpanhes, saying,
“Take great stones in your hand, and hide them in mortar in the brick work, which is at the entry of Pharaoh’s house in Tahpanhes, in the sight of the men of Judah;

and tell them, Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, says: ‘Behold, I will send and take Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant, and will set his throne on these stones that I have hidden; and he shall spread his royal pavilion over them.
He will come, and will strike the land of Egypt; such as are for death shall be put to death, and such as are for captivity to captivity, and such as are for the sword to the sword.

I will kindle a fire in the houses of the gods of Egypt; and he shall burn them, and carry them away captive: and he shall array himself with the land of Egypt, as a shepherd puts on his garment; and he shall go out from there in peace.
He shall also break the pillars of Beth Shemesh, that is in the land of Egypt; and he shall burn the houses of the gods of Egypt with fire.’”

footnotes.content: Jeremiah has spoken all the words Yahweh gave him—faithfully, completely, holding nothing back. Notice the repetition: 'all the words,' 'all these words.' The prophet's obedience was perfect, even though he knew rejection was coming. We serve a God who speaks; our task is to listen and speak truly, whatever the cost.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Azariah and Johanan—'the proud men'—stand up and call Jeremiah a liar. They accuse him of speaking falsely about Yahweh's will. Here is the pattern: when God's word opposes what we've already decided, we often question the messenger's honesty rather than examine our own hearts. Pride speaks first, and it calls truth a lie.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They blame Baruch, Jeremiah's scribe, for turning the prophet against them. In desperate moments, we reach for scapegoats. Easier to fault a secretary than face the truth that Yahweh Himself has said 'stay in the land.' Yet God often works through unexpected people—and our dismissal of them shows how far our hearts have drifted from Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The captains of the forces and all the people refuse to obey Yahweh's voice. Here is the tragedy plain: they hear the word clearly, yet choose rebellion. Obedience begins with listening, but it requires will—the courage to do what Yahweh says even when every human instinct screams otherwise. By the end of this verse, the door closes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Johanan takes 'all the remnant of Judah'—families who had escaped death, exile, and loss. They were the survivors, the spared ones. Yet even those whom Yahweh had preserved now turn from Him. Sometimes the Lord's mercy toward us is not received as mercy, but as license to choose our own way.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Notice whom they took: the men, the women, the children, the king's daughters, Jeremiah, and Baruch. The prophet goes into Egypt not by his own will but dragged along by rebels. And Baruch—the faithful scribe, falsely blamed—goes too. The innocent suffer alongside the willful. Yet the Lord sees both of them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They came into Egypt—to Tahpanhes, one of Egypt's chief cities. 'They didn't obey Yahweh's voice.' The refrain echoes through this chapter like a funeral bell. Now they are in the place where Yahweh swore they should not go. Geography and disobedience are joined forever now.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even in Egypt—the place of their rebellion—Yahweh's word still comes to Jeremiah. The Lord does not abandon His prophet when His people have abandoned His voice. Jeremiah remains faithful not because the remnant believed, but because he belongs to Yahweh. The word finds him even among the disobedient.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh commands a strange sign: Jeremiah must take great stones and hide them in mortar at Pharaoh's house in Tahpanhes, witnessed by the men of Judah. This is a prophetic act—the stones will become the foundation of Nebuchadnezzar's throne. The people see it. They cannot unsee it. God makes His judgment visible.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Nebuchadnezzar is called 'my servant'—a title that stuns us. Yet from Yahweh's perspective, the king of Babylon becomes an instrument of judgment, even unknowingly. The Lord uses earthly powers to accomplish His purposes. His throne will be set upon the very stones Jeremiah hides. Nothing escapes the Father's hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Death, captivity, the sword—each person receives according to what awaits them. There is a terrible sorting: the Lord knows what each person deserves. Yet even in judgment, His word is true. The people thought Egypt would be sanctuary. Instead, Egypt becomes the place where judgment overtakes them. Yahweh's reach is longer than any border.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh will kindle a fire in the houses of Egypt's gods and burn them. Here is the judgment on idolatry itself. The remnant fled to Egypt perhaps hoping to find gods who would shelter them there—but Yahweh's judgment reaches even the idols. Only He is God. The fire that purifies will also consume false hopes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The pillars of Beth Shemesh, the houses of Egypt's gods—all will be broken and burned. Readers today hear an echo of this: how many certainties have we built on pillars we thought unshakeable? The Lord's patient judgment on our idols—the things we trust instead of Him—is also thorough. Yet even judgment is merciful in its honesty: it breaks what was already broken.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
